issues.legal_issue: A rent-reduction determination classifying land cannot rest solely on a register entry concerning another village when there is no evidence that the villages are similar.
material_facts: The officer classified the lands using a report that relied on a settlement-register entry concerning the soil of a different village.
There was no corresponding settlement-register entry for the village in question and no evidence establishing that its soil was similar to that of the other village.
The officer did not conduct an adequate village-specific inquiry into the relevant land conditions.
issues.conclusion: The officer’s determination was based on no relevant evidence and violated fundamental principles of judicial procedure; the resulting government notification was not a valid order under the statutory rent-fixing power and was struck down.
issues.legal_principle: The statutory scheme required the Special Officer to determine the relevant rent rates for each village and class of land on relevant material. A determination based solely on an unrelated village’s register entry, without evidence connecting that entry to the village under inquiry, has no rational evidentiary basis. The Court referred to O. K. Muthuswamy Mudaliar v. State of Madras in considering the significance of actual land conditions, including cultivation and irrigation, rather than registration alone.

predicates.rent_reduction_proceeding: An authority is determining land classes or rent rates in a proceeding to reduce rents.
predicates.village_specific_land_classification_req: The determination concerns the classification of land in a particular village.
predicates.determination_based_only_on_other_villag: The authority relied only on a register entry concerning land in a different village.
predicates.no_evidence_of_village_similarity: No evidence showed that the relevant land conditions in the two villages were similar.

issues.definition: When a rent-reduction determination for a village rests only on another village’s register entry and no evidence establishes that the villages are similar, the resulting rent-reduction order is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory bar on challenging rent-fixing orders does not exclude civil court jurisdiction over a challenge to an order made without relevant evidence and in violation of fundamental principles of judicial procedure.
material_facts: A civil suit challenged a government notification fixing reduced rents for land in a village.

The notification rested on the Special Officer’s determination, which was based solely on a settlement-register entry for a different village and lacked relevant evidence connecting that entry to the village in question.
The statute barred court challenges to orders made under its rent-fixing provision.
issues.conclusion: The statutory bar did not apply to the impugned notification, and civil court jurisdiction to entertain the challenge was not excluded.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 8(1), an order made under section 3(2) was not liable to be questioned in court. But the exclusion of civil court jurisdiction is not readily inferred, and even where jurisdiction is excluded, courts may examine whether statutory provisions were complied with and whether the tribunal acted in conformity with fundamental principles of judicial procedure. The Court applied Secretary of State v. Mask and Company and followed Dhulabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh; it also referred to O. K. Muthuswamy Mudaliar v. State of Madras.

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_rent_fixing_order: A plaintiff brings a civil suit challenging an order fixing reduced rents.
predicates.order_based_on_determination_without_rel: The challenged order rests on an administrative determination that lacks relevant evidentiary support.
predicates.determination_violated_fundamental_proce: The determination was made in a way that violated fundamental principles of judicial procedure.

issues.definition: When a civil suit challenges a rent-fixing order resting on a determination unsupported by relevant evidence and made in violation of fundamental procedure, civil courts retain jurisdiction to hear the challenge.
